title: The Writing on the Palace Wall
overview: At a drunken royal feast, a mysterious hand writes a message on the wall announcing that the king's reign is over, and that same night Babylon falls.

parts.label: A feast with temple cups (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Babylon's king throws a huge party and has his guests drink from the gold and silver cups taken from the Jerusalem temple decades earlier, while they praise idols. Turning objects set apart for Israel's God into party ware was a deliberate insult, not a careless choice.

parts.label: The hand on the wall (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: A hand appears and writes on the palace plaster near the lamp, and the king is so terrified his legs give way. His experts cannot read or explain it; the reward of becoming third ruler probably reflects that Belshazzar himself ruled as second, under his absent father Nabonidus.

parts.label: The queen remembers Daniel (vv. 10-16)
parts.note: The queen, probably the king's mother, recalls Daniel, the Jewish exile who interpreted dreams for Nebuchadnezzar. Calling Nebuchadnezzar Belshazzar's "father" likely means ancestor or royal predecessor, a common way of speaking at the time.

parts.label: Daniel's blunt rebuke (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: Daniel turns down the gifts and reminds the king how Nebuchadnezzar's pride led to his humiliation, as told in chapter 4. Belshazzar knew that story yet still mocked the God on whom his whole life depends, and the writing is the answer to that.

parts.label: Numbered, weighed, divided (vv. 25-28)
parts.note: The three words mean roughly numbered, weighed and divided, and Daniel reads each as a verdict: your days are counted, you have been weighed and found too light, your kingdom is split and handed to the Medes and Persians. Some scholars also hear names of weights or coins in the words, though that is debated, and peres sounds like the word for Persia.

parts.label: That same night (vv. 29-31)
parts.note: Daniel receives his honors, and that night the king is killed as Babylon falls to the Medes and Persians, which history dates to 539 BC. Darius the Mede is not known from records outside the Bible, and scholars still debate who he was.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter is a straightforward historical report from the sixth century BC or a story shaped later to encourage Jews living under hostile rulers, though both read it as a warning about arrogant power.
think: When someone has clearly seen where pride led people before them, what do you think makes it so hard for them to learn from it?
